title: Case Report: Weakness and Recurrent Falls in an Older Patient
case_prompt:
An 82-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, surgically treated small bowel carcinoid tumor (15 years prior), latent tuberculosis, hypothyroidism, and hypertension was transferred for progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness and frequent falls. Over the past four months she had three prior admissions for similar symptoms without a diagnosis. 

On the first admission, she had seven days of vertical and horizontal diplopia, mild vertigo, right-eye ptosis, left facial droop, decreased right hemi-body sensation to light touch, and right lower-extremity weakness. Laboratory tests, including thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, inflammatory markers, and creatine phosphokinase, were within normal limits. Brain CT and MRI showed no acute findings.

During the second admission, she experienced severe bilateral leg weakness with back pain on ambulation and a left facial droop. MRI of the head, neck, and lumbar spine revealed only advanced degenerative disk disease and moderate spinal stenosis without acute pathology.

On the third admission, she presented after multiple falls associated with presyncope. She developed diarrhea and was treated for campylobacteriosis. She again had a left facial droop; repeat head CT and CTA were negative for ischemia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed hypoglycorrhachia, elevated protein, and lymphocytic pleocytosis without oligoclonal bands or malignant cells. CSF culture grew Propionibacterium acnes, and she received two weeks of ampicillin without improvement.

A third lumbar puncture revealed a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold and elevated β-(1,3)-D-glucan but negative CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus I and II, varicella, West Nile virus, and tuberculosis; negative fungal and acid-fast bacillus stains and cultures; negative VDRL; and negative cryptococcal antigen and brucella titers. Serum tests were negative for brucella, coxsackie, and HIV. CSF Lyme IgG and IgM were elevated. Autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panels, complement levels, and thyroid studies were unremarkable. Screening for recurrent carcinoid (24-h urine 5-HIAA, serum serotonin, chromogranin A, gastrin, and vasoactive intestinal peptide) and abdominal imaging were normal. She underwent penicillin desensitization and completed a course of IVIG without clinical response.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hypothyroid-related myopathy was considered — “her free T4 was normal and her TSH level remained below 10 uIU/mL ... therefore, hypothyroid-related myopathy was also deemed unlikely.”  
2. Autoimmune myopathies, myasthenia gravis, and Lambert–Eaton syndrome were considered — “most of these autoimmune conditions tend to affect all limbs equally and symmetrically.”  
3. Myasthenia gravis was further excluded — “testing was negative for anti-voltage-gated antibody and anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody, decreasing the likelihood of disorders such as myasthenia gravis.”  
4. Guillain–Barré syndrome was considered — “GBS treatment was initiated with IVIG ... failed to show any improvement.”  
5. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy was considered — “increased white blood cells in CSF are not typical ... clinically, she did not present as a traditional CIDP patient, given that her weakness spared her upper extremities.”  
6. Transverse myelitis was considered — “TM is associated with symptoms corresponding to a spinal cord level and typically involves symmetrical paralysis ... our patient had asymmetric syndromes ... therefore, TM was an unlikely etiology.”  
7. Bell’s palsy was considered — “Bell’s palsy was deemed unlikely, given that the CSF PCR was negative for infectious agents associated with Bell’s palsy.”  
8. Tuberculous meningitis was considered — “CSF PCR results for ... tuberculosis were all negative ... thus TB was unlikely.”  
9. Fungal meningitis was considered — “culture and staining were negative for fungus ... Therefore, a fungal infection was unlikely.”  
10. Lyme neuroborreliosis was considered — “CSF Lyme antibodies were positive ... despite completing ... penicillin, she failed to show a clinical improvement.”  
11. Recurrent carcinoid or paraneoplastic neuropathy was considered — “levels of gastrin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and 5-hydroxytryptamine ... were all within normal limits, and abdominal imaging lacked findings suggestive of neuroendocrine tumor recurrence.”  
12. Leptomeningeal tumor spread was favored — “given the CSF lumbar puncture results showed hypoglycorrhachia and elevated protein ... and, given that infectious causes were ruled out, carcinomatosis meningoencephalitis was considered a likely diagnosis.”
